title: Browser & OS
whyItMatters: The machinery under the framework: what the process, the thread and the event loop are actually doing while your code runs.

questions.prompt: What do two threads in the same process share that two processes do not?
options: The CPU core they run on
The same address space and heap
The same call stack
The same file descriptors only
questions.explanation: Threads share the process's memory, which is what makes them cheap to switch between and dangerous to write to concurrently.

concept.title: Process vs thread
concept.summary: The difference is memory isolation, and everything else follows from it.
points: Each process has its own address space; a crash cannot corrupt another.
Threads inside a process share the heap, so they need locks.
Each thread still gets its own stack and registers.
Modern browsers isolate renderer work across processes, often by site, to limit the impact of crashes and compromised pages.

questions.prompt: A click handler schedules `setTimeout(f, 0)` and then resolves a promise with `.then(g)`. Which runs first?
options: f, because it was scheduled first
g, because microtasks drain before the next task
They run in parallel
Whichever the browser decides that tick
questions.explanation: The microtask queue is drained completely after the current task, before any timer callback is taken from the task queue.

concept.title: Two queues, not one
concept.summary: Microtasks are not just faster timers — they run at a different point in the loop.
points: Tasks: timers, events, I/O. One is taken per loop turn.
Microtasks: promise callbacks, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver.
After each task, the entire microtask queue drains — including ones added while draining.
An endlessly self-queueing microtask starves the loop and freezes the page.

questions.prompt: Which change forces layout (reflow) rather than only paint?
options: Changing an element's background-color
Changing an element's width
Changing an element's opacity
Changing an element's box-shadow colour
questions.explanation: Width changes geometry, so positions must be recomputed. Colour and opacity do not move anything.

concept.title: Style → layout → paint → composite
concept.summary: The further up the pipeline your change lands, the more work it costs.
points: Geometry (width, top, font-size) triggers layout, then paint, then composite.
Colour and shadow skip layout but still repaint.
transform and opacity can be handled by the compositor alone.
Reading offsetHeight after a write forces a synchronous layout — the classic thrash.

questions.prompt: Why does a long synchronous loop freeze the page rather than just delaying itself?
options: The browser deprioritises long-running scripts
Rendering and event handling share the same thread as your script
The garbage collector pauses the page
The loop consumes the microtask queue
questions.explanation: Script, layout, paint and event dispatch all run on the main thread, so a busy loop leaves no turn for any of them.

concept.title: One thread does everything visible
concept.summary: Blocking it blocks the whole page, not just your code.
points: Script execution, layout, paint and event handlers share the main thread.
Nothing renders until the current task yields.
Web Workers get their own thread but no DOM access.
Breaking work into chunks across tasks keeps the page responsive.

questions.prompt: What actually happens to an object you `postMessage` to a Web Worker?
options: The worker receives a reference to the same object
It is structured-cloned, so the worker gets a copy
It is serialised to JSON and parsed
It is shared only if it is frozen
questions.explanation: Structured clone copies the object, which is why workers cannot corrupt main-thread state — and why sending a large object is not free.

concept.title: Workers copy, they do not share
concept.summary: Isolation is the whole point, and the copy is the price.
points: Structured clone handles Maps, Sets, Dates and cycles — unlike JSON.
Cloning a large payload costs real main-thread time.
Transferables (ArrayBuffer) move ownership instead of copying.
SharedArrayBuffer is the only true shared memory, and it needs COOP/COEP headers.

questions.prompt: What lives on the stack rather than the heap?
options: Every object your program allocates
The call frames and local references of running functions
Anything declared with const
Strings, because they are immutable
questions.explanation: The stack holds call frames and their local slots; objects themselves live on the heap and the frame holds a reference.

concept.title: Stack frames, heap objects
concept.summary: The stack unwinds automatically; the heap needs a collector.
points: Each call pushes a frame with its locals and return address.
Objects, arrays and closures are allocated on the heap.
Return pops the frame instantly — no collection needed.
Unbounded recursion overflows the stack long before the heap fills.

questions.prompt: What makes an object eligible for garbage collection?
options: Its variable went out of scope
It is no longer reachable from any root
Its reference count reached zero
It has not been read for a full GC cycle
questions.explanation: Modern engines trace reachability from roots. Reference counting alone cannot collect cycles, which is why it is not used on its own.

concept.title: Reachability, not scope
concept.summary: Leaks are almost always something still holding a reference.
points: Roots are the global object and the active call stacks.
Anything reachable from a root survives, however unused.
Two objects referencing only each other are still collected — the cycle is unreachable.
Detached DOM nodes held by a listener or closure are the classic browser leak.

questions.prompt: JavaScript is single-threaded, so how does a fetch happen at the same time as your code?
expects: separates the JS thread from the browser's other threads
describes the callback being queued, not run immediately
names the event loop taking it once the stack is empty
questions.probeIfMissing: Which part of that work is actually running in JavaScript?

concept.title: Single-threaded JS, multi-threaded browser
concept.summary: The concurrency is real; it just is not happening in your code.
points: The network request is handled by the browser, not the JS thread.
When it completes, the callback is pushed onto a queue.
The event loop only takes from that queue when the stack is empty.
So your code is never interrupted mid-function — it just resumes later.

questions.prompt: Why does a browser put each tab in its own process when threads would be cheaper?
expects: names memory or security isolation between sites
acknowledges the memory cost as the tradeoff
questions.probeIfMissing: What would one tab be able to do to another if they shared memory?

concept.title: Paying memory for isolation
concept.summary: The cost is deliberate and the reason is security first.
points: A crash or an out-of-memory kill takes down one tab, not the browser.
Separate address spaces mean one site cannot read another's memory.
Spectre made that hardware-level, not just policy — hence site isolation.
The price is real: each process carries its own heap and engine state.

questions.prompt: A list scrolls smoothly with 50 rows and stutters at 5000. Walk me through where you look.
expects: distinguishes work per frame from work per item
names a concrete tool or measurement before a fix
reaches a structural fix such as virtualisation rather than micro-optimising
questions.probeIfMissing: What is being done 5000 times that was only done 50 times before?

concept.title: Reading a stutter
concept.summary: A frame budget is about 16ms. Find what exceeds it before changing anything.
points: Record a performance profile during the stutter — do not guess.
Long layout or paint bars point at DOM size; long script bars at your code.
Scroll handlers doing layout reads per event are a common cause.
5000 rows in the DOM is usually the answer: virtualise, do not micro-optimise.

questions.prompt: A single-page app grows to a gigabyte of memory after an hour of navigation. What are you looking for?
expects: names something still holding references after unmount
gives a concrete example such as a listener, timer or subscription
mentions heap snapshots or detached nodes as the way to confirm
questions.probeIfMissing: What could still be pointing at a component that is no longer on screen?

concept.title: The leak is always a reference
concept.summary: Nothing is collected while a root can still reach it.
points: Listeners on window or document outlive the component that added them.
An uncleaned interval keeps its whole closure alive forever.
Detached DOM nodes held by a closure show up clearly in a heap snapshot.
Compare two snapshots taken minutes apart and look at what grew.
